title: Introduction to EF Core
description: Discover Entity Framework Core, the official ORM for .NET, and learn how it bridges the gap between your C# object models and relational databases.

blocks.text: Entity Framework Core, or EF Core for short, is an object-relational mapper (ORM) that lets you work with databases using .NET objects. Instead of writing raw SQL queries and manually mapping results to classes, EF Core handles the translation between your C# code and the database for you.

When you use EF Core, you define your data model as C# classes called entities. Each entity represents a table in the database, and each property on the class represents a column. EF Core then takes care of creating tables, inserting data, querying records, updating rows, and deleting entries — all through LINQ queries or method-based APIs.
EF Core is the recommended data access technology for new .NET applications. It is lightweight, extensible, and supports SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and many other database providers.

blocks.title: EF Core vs. Dapper
blocks.text: EF Core is a full-featured ORM with change tracking, migrations, and lazy loading. Dapper is a micro-ORM focused on raw SQL performance with minimal abstraction. Many production applications use both: EF Core for standard CRUD and Dapper for high-performance reporting queries.

The central class in EF Core is DbContext. Think of DbContext as a session with the database — it tracks changes to your entities, manages connections, and translates LINQ queries into SQL. Every entity set you want to query or save is exposed as a DbSet<T> on the context.

blocks.title: A simple DbContext with one entity
blocks.content: This DbContext exposes a DbSet for the Product entity and configures the database connection.

blocks.text: The Product class is a plain C# class with no EF Core-specific base classes or attributes required. EF Core uses conventions: a property named 'Id' or '<ClassName>Id' is automatically treated as the primary key. The DbSet<Product> property provides the entry point for all Product-related database operations.
How EF Core Translates Code to SQL

One of the most powerful features of EF Core is LINQ query translation. You write queries using familiar C# syntax, and EF Core converts them into optimized SQL at runtime. This means you can work with strongly-typed objects instead of string-based SQL queries.

blocks.title: LINQ query translated to SQL
blocks.content: Querying active products under a price threshold using LINQ methods.

blocks.text: This LINQ query is translated by EF Core into SQL similar to 'SELECT Name, Price FROM Products WHERE IsActive = 1 AND Price < 50 ORDER BY Name'. You never have to write that SQL yourself. EF Core also handles parameterization automatically, protecting against SQL injection attacks.

blocks.title: Important: LINQ queries are parameterized automatically
blocks.text: EF Core automatically converts LINQ parameters into SQL parameters, which prevents SQL injection. Do not concatenate user input into raw SQL strings — always use parameterized queries through LINQ or FromSqlInterpolated.
Adding EF Core to Your Project

To use EF Core, you need to install two NuGet packages: the core EF Core package and a provider package for your database. The provider package contains the database-specific SQL generator and type mappings.

blocks.title: NuGet packages for common databases
items: Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite — for SQLite, great for development and testing
Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.InMemory — for unit testing with an in-memory database

blocks.title: Installing EF Core packages via .NET CLI
blocks.content: Install the SQL Server provider and tools packages.
blocks.code:
dotnet add package Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer
dotnet add package Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Tools

blocks.text: The Tools package provides the 'dotnet ef' CLI commands for creating migrations and updating the database schema. It is not needed at runtime, only during development.

EF Core supports all four standard database operations: Create, Read, Update, and Delete. Each operation is performed through the DbSet<T> on your DbContext. EF Core tracks entity states automatically, so you only need to call SaveChangesAsync to persist modifications.

blocks.title: Basic CRUD with DbSet<T>
items: Create: Instantiate a new entity and call context.Add(entity), then SaveChangesAsync()
Read: Query with LINQ using Where, FirstOrDefault, ToListAsync, and other methods
Update: Retrieve the entity, modify its properties, then call SaveChangesAsync()
Delete: Retrieve the entity, call context.Remove(entity), then SaveChangesAsync()

blocks.title: Full CRUD example
blocks.content: Creating, reading, updating, and deleting products using EF Core.

blocks.title: Tip: Always use async methods
blocks.text: Use the async database operations like ToListAsync(), FirstOrDefaultAsync(), and SaveChangesAsync() in web applications. Async database calls free up threads to handle other requests, improving scalability under load.

terms.definition: Object-Relational Mapper — a library that maps between database tables and .NET objects, eliminating the need for raw SQL and manual mapping.
The main EF Core class responsible for database interaction, tracking entity changes, and coordinating queries and saves.
A property on DbContext that represents a database table and provides query and CRUD operations for entity type T.
A C# class that maps to a database table. Its properties map to columns.
EF Core's default behavior of inferring table names, primary keys, and column types from entity class names and property types.

blocks.title: Create Your First EF Core Model
blocks.description: Set up a new project with EF Core, define an entity model, and perform CRUD operations against a SQLite database.
steps: Create a new console project: 'dotnet new console -n EfCoreIntro'
Define a Book entity class with Id, Title, Author, PublishedYear, and Price properties
Define a LibraryDbContext that inherits from DbContext with a DbSet<Book> property
Override OnConfiguring to use UseSqlite with a local database file 'library.db'
In Program.cs, ensure the database is created and insert three sample books
Query the books with a LINQ Where clause and print titles and prices to the console
blocks.expectedOutcome: Three books are inserted into the SQLite database. The console output shows the titles and prices of all books published after 2015, proving the LINQ query was translated to SQL correctly.

items.text: I understand the role of DbContext and DbSet<T>
items.hint: DbContext is the session; DbSet<T> is the table entry point.

items.text: I can install EF Core and a database provider via NuGet
items.hint: You need both the core package and a provider like SqlServer or Sqlite.

items.hint: A property named 'Id' or '<TypeName>Id' is automatically the primary key.

items.hint: Add, Find, FirstOrDefault, Remove, and SaveChangesAsync are the core methods.

items.text: I understand why EF Core protects against SQL injection
items.hint: LINQ queries are translated into parameterized SQL automatically.

blocks.title: EF Core Introduction Summary
points: EF Core is an ORM that maps C# classes to database tables and properties to columns
DbContext is the central class for all database interactions and change tracking
DbSet<T> provides query and CRUD access to a specific entity type
EF Core uses conventions to infer keys, table names, and column types automatically
LINQ queries are translated to SQL at runtime with automatic parameterization
NuGet packages for both the core EF Core library and your database provider are required
blocks.takeaway: Entity Framework Core dramatically simplifies database access by letting you work with C# objects instead of raw SQL. Understanding DbContext, DbSet, and the LINQ query pipeline is the foundation for everything else in this module.
